blocks.text: The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to a network of physical devices connected through the internet that can collect, share, and act on data. These devices often include sensors, processors, and communication hardware, allowing them to work together intelligently. IoT connects everyday objects such as lights, thermostats, and appliances so they can be monitored and controlled remotely. This interconnection helps improve efficiency, convenience, and real-time decision-making in daily life and industrial operations.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: The IoT connects everyday devices like fridges, cars, and lights so they can “talk” to each other automatically.

IoT systems operate by linking devices through wireless communication technologies like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or cellular networks. Each connected device communicates with others or a central platform to exchange information automatically. This continuous interaction creates a smart environment where machines and systems work together with minimal human effort.

In smart homes, IoT enables residents to control lighting, heating, curtains, and security systems through mobile applications or voice commands, as shown in Figure 8.3. For example, smart LED bulbs can be turned on or off through a smartphone, set to turn on automatically at 6:00 p.m. Similarly, smart curtains or blinds can open automatically with the morning alarm and close when the room temperature rises above 35°C to help keep the room cool. A smart thermostat can also adjust temperature based on user preferences, while security cameras can send alerts directly to smartphones. These systems not only add comfort but also help conserve energy and improve safety.

In healthcare, IoT sensors can monitor patient conditions such as heart rate, blood pressure, or glucose levels in real time. This allows doctors to track patient health remotely and respond quickly in emergencies. Similarly, in agriculture, IoT devices measure soil moisture, temperature, and weather patterns to optimize irrigation and crop management, increasing yield and reducing waste.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Smart homes, wearable fitness bands, and smart farms are all powered by IoT technology.

blocks.alt: On the left three input sensors (temperature, motion and light) feed a controller, a microcontroller such as an ESP32. The controller exchanges data with the Internet or cloud, which connects to a mobile app and to three output actuators on the right: smart light, smart fan and smart socket. A note gives example rules: lights on at 6:00 p.m., curtains close above 35 C, cameras send alerts to the phone.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.3: Smart Home using IoT: Connected devices such as lights, thermostat, and security systems can be monitored and controlled remotely through the internet. (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.3)
blocks.long_description: Sensors sense, the controller and cloud decide, and actuators act; the phone app lets the user watch and override the system.
